Ecosystem · honest landscape

You already run some of these. Baltor is the layer they’re missing.

Most teams compose a context stack from several open-source tools — memory graphs, tracing, eval, a data catalog. They’re good at what they do. But every one of them retrieves or measures what it’s given — none decide whether a fact is authoritative, current, and safe to serve. That governance layer is the consensus gap, and it’s what Baltor is. This is where it fits beside the tools you know.

The open-source context stack

Representative projects · Baltor composes with each

The gap none of them fill

Memory graphs relate facts. Tracing and eval measure quality. Catalogs govern internal access and lineage. None of them verify a fact against the external authority in force, hold out the contradiction, and serve it with a receipt. That triad is Baltor — and it’s why Baltor sits upstream of retrieval, not inside it.

Verify vs the authority
The regulation, standard or contract in force — not the freshest internal copy.
no OSS tool does this
Hold out the conflict
The losing value is surfaced separately, never served — truth is ranked, not deleted.
no OSS tool does this
Serve with a receipt
Every served fact carries a signed receipt + source handle, agent- and model-neutral.
no OSS tool does this

Designed to interoperate, not replace

Baltor is the governed layer your existing tools read from
Keep your catalog & lineage
Baltor records lineage as standards-shaped events your data catalog can ingest — it governs correctness above the catalog, not instead of it.
Keep your observability
Serve/verify receipts export as traces your LLM-observability tool can read — Baltor adds the “was it true?” layer over the “what happened?” layer.
Keep your eval harness
Verification is evidence, not authority — it composes with RAG-eval frameworks (and the open OpenBenchmarkHub), never replaces the gate.
An honest landscape. The projects named here are real, strong tools doing real work; Baltor composes with them and fills the verification-governance gap they leave — it is not a catalog, a tracer, or an eval framework. Interoperability shown here is the design intent of these prototypes, not a shipped integration list. Not legal, medical, or financial advice — the source in force is the authority; Baltor preserves its citation and receipt. See the engine and the fragile-context atlas.
